name: Outcome Bias
description: After the result is known, people judge a past decision by how it turned out instead of by whether it was a good decision given the information available at the time. A lucky bad process can look wise, and a sound process with a bad result can look foolish.
design_relevance_note: Highly relevant to product postmortems, experiment readouts, roadmap bets, and research synthesis: teams can unfairly regrade earlier decisions after a launch succeeds or fails, which corrupts learning about decision quality.
prevalence_note: Common in decision-quality, forecasting, medicine, investing, and product-postmortem discussions, even if less famous in mainstream UX lore than hindsight bias or anchoring.

findings.description: When evaluating past decisions, people rated the very same decision process as better when it led to a good outcome and worse when it led to a bad outcome, even though outcome quality was not a clean indicator of how sound the original decision process was. Baron and Hershey named this distortion 'outcome bias.'
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

applications.title: NBA coaches are 17 percentage points more likely to change their lineup after a close loss than a close win
applications.description: A peer-reviewed study of over 20,000 NBA games (Lefgren, Platt & Price, 2014, Management Science, 'Sticking with What (Barely) Worked: A Test of Outcome Bias') found coaches are 17 percent more likely to change their starting lineup in the game following a one-point loss than after a one-point win, even though a team's win rate in the surrounding games is nearly identical whether it won or lost that game by one point -- evidence that coaches react to the binary outcome of a close game rather than to the actual information it carries about their strategy, including reacting to factors entirely outside their control such as the opposing team's free-throw luck.
applications.ethical_note: This documents a real, rigorously quantified instance of outcome bias in organizational decision-making -- coaches, and by extension the front offices that judge them -- with no persuasion or product-design dimension. Included because it is one of the most cleanly measured real-world instances of this specific bias available, backed by a large disclosed dataset and peer-reviewed publication rather than an anecdotal claim.
